title: Frequent Nosebleeds in Adults: Causes, When to Worry, and Blood Tests
summary: Frequent nosebleeds usually come from dry, irritated vessels in the nose. Learn when to worry, signs of a bleeding problem and the blood tests to check.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


Most frequent nosebleeds in adults come from small blood vessels at the front of the nose that dry out or get irritated. Dry air, colds, allergies, nose picking, hard nose blowing and blood-thinning medicines are the usual reasons \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. Nosebleeds are common: at least 60% of people in the United States have one at some point, and about 6% of those who do seek medical care for it \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \].


A few patterns point beyond the nose. Nosebleeds that come often, last longer than 10 minutes, need packing or cautery to stop, or come with easy bruising or heavy periods can be a sign of a bleeding disorder \[[3](https://www.cdc.gov/von-willebrand/about/index.html) \]. This page covers when to get urgent care, how to stop a nosebleed, the common causes, and which blood tests check for a bleeding cause, including what a normal result cannot rule out. It is about adults. For a child with frequent nosebleeds, contact their provider \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].


## When a nosebleed needs urgent care


Get emergency care for a nosebleed when \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]:


- the bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes of pressure
- it follows a head injury
- your nose may be broken
- you take a blood-thinning medicine
- earlier nosebleeds needed treatment from a specialist to stop


Contact your doctor, rather than the emergency room, if you have frequent nosebleeds, if they start without a cold or other irritation, or if they follow sinus or other surgery \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].


## How to stop a nosebleed


Sit up, lean slightly forward and breathe through your mouth, so blood runs out of the nose rather than down your throat. Pinch the soft lower part of your nose firmly shut and hold it for a full 10 minutes before checking whether it has stopped \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. The clinical guideline for nosebleeds describes the same thing: firm, sustained pressure on the lower third of the nose for at least 5 minutes \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \].


Do not lie down, and do not pack the inside of the nose with gauze. A cold compress across the bridge of the nose may help. Once it stops, avoid sniffing or blowing your nose for several hours \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].


## What causes nosebleeds in adults


Most nosebleeds start on the front part of the septum, the wall between the nostrils, where small vessels sit close to the surface. These are usually easy to stop \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. The common causes are:


- **Dry or cold air.** Heated indoor air in winter dries the lining of the nose \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].
- **Colds, allergies and sinus problems,** including repeated sneezing and nose blowing \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].
- **Nose picking and minor injuries** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].
- **Nasal sprays and devices.** Overusing decongestant nasal sprays and using nasal oxygen tubing can both irritate the lining \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].
- **Snorted drugs or chemical irritants,** including cocaine \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].
- **Blood-thinning medicines** such as warfarin, clopidogrel and aspirin, which can cause or worsen nosebleeds \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].


Less common causes include a deviated septum, recent sinus or other nose surgery, and a growth in the nose or sinuses \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. Repeated nosebleeds can also be a sign of high blood pressure or a bleeding disorder \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. Each of those has its own section below.


## Signs frequent nosebleeds may be a bleeding problem


A bleeding disorder means the blood does not clot as it should. Its usual signs are easy bruising, heavy periods and nosebleeds that happen often \[[4](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/bleeding-disorders) \]. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, found in up to 1% of people in the United States \[[3](https://www.cdc.gov/von-willebrand/about/index.html) \].


The CDC describes the nosebleeds that raise concern for von Willebrand disease as ones that \[[3](https://www.cdc.gov/von-willebrand/about/index.html) \]:


- happen often, usually five times or more in a year
- last more than 10 minutes
- need packing or cautery to stop


Other features add weight to the same question:


- **Bleeding somewhere else too,** such as easy bruising or longer than normal bleeding after a cut, dental work, surgery or childbirth \[[3](https://www.cdc.gov/von-willebrand/about/index.html) \].
- **Heavy periods,** meaning soaking through a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours on the heaviest days, bleeding that lasts longer than 7 days, or flooding \[[3](https://www.cdc.gov/von-willebrand/about/index.html) \].
- **A family history** of a bleeding disorder \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \].
- **A blood thinner or antiplatelet medicine,** which the nosebleed guideline asks clinicians to record alongside personal and family bleeding history \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \].


Nosebleeds on their own, from one nostril, that follow a cold or a dry week and stop with 10 minutes of pressure, fit the common local causes above much better than a bleeding disorder.


## Which blood tests check for a bleeding cause


Blood tests do not look inside the nose. What they can check is whether your blood counts and clotting are normal, and whether repeated bleeding has drained your iron. The table maps each pattern to the test to start with and the limit of a normal result.


Pattern Test to start with What a normal result cannot rule out


Frequent nosebleeds with bruising, bleeding gums or tiny red skin spots[CBC with differential and platelet count](https://mitohealth.com/products/complete-blood-count-cbc-with-differential-and-platelet-count) Platelets that are present in normal numbers but do not work properly


Long or hard-to-stop bleeds, or a known liver problem[PT with INR and PTT](https://mitohealth.com/products/prothrombin-time-with-inr-pt-and-partial-thromboplastin-time-ptt) Von Willebrand disease, which can leave both results normal


Lifelong bleeding, heavy periods, or relatives with the same[Von Willebrand factor antigen](https://mitohealth.com/products/von-willebrand-factor-antigen-vwf) , as one part of a fuller workup Von Willebrand disease, because levels vary and one normal result does not exclude it


Heavy alcohol use or known liver disease[Hepatic function panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/liver-profile) , with PT/INR A clotting problem, because the liver panel itself does not measure clotting time


Repeated bleeding with tiredness or breathlessness[Ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/products/ferritin) , or the[Anemia Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/anemia-panel-b) Low iron stores when inflammation is raising ferritin


### Complete blood count: platelets and anemia


Platelets form the first plug when a small vessel breaks, and nosebleeds are one of the listed symptoms of a low platelet count \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/platelet-tests/) \]. A complete blood count with differential and platelet count is the sensible first test, because the same draw shows whether you have too few platelets and whether repeated bleeding has made you anemic. For what the marker measures, see[platelet count](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/platelet-count) , and for the causes of a low count and what different levels mean, see our guide to[low platelet symptoms](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-platelets) . If the count is the only question, the narrower[platelet count blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/platelet-count) measures it on its own.


Where it stops: a platelet count counts platelets. It does not test how well they work, which needs separate platelet function tests \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/platelet-tests/) \]. It also says nothing about the clotting factors.


### PT with INR and PTT: clotting time


Prothrombin time (PT, reported with the INR) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) each measure how long blood takes to clot, through a different group of clotting factors. PT/INR is used to investigate unexplained bleeding such as unusually heavy nosebleeds, to check for liver problems or low vitamin K, and to monitor warfarin \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prothrombin-time-test-and-inr-ptinr/) \]. PTT checks the clotting factors PT does not, and the two are usually read together \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/partial-thromboplastin-time-ptt-test/) \]. A prolonged PTT can point to hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, liver disease, low vitamin K or a blood thinner \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/partial-thromboplastin-time-ptt-test/) \].


Where it stops: an abnormal result does not by itself mean you have a condition, and more tests usually follow \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/partial-thromboplastin-time-ptt-test/) \]. A normal pair does not close the question either. Von Willebrand disease can leave both results normal, so a convincing bleeding history still needs von Willebrand testing \[[8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39556633/) \]\[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33570651/) \]. The[PT with INR and PTT test](https://mitohealth.com/products/prothrombin-time-with-inr-pt-and-partial-thromboplastin-time-ptt) covers both in one draw. A[PT with INR test](https://mitohealth.com/products/prothrombin-time-inr-pt) on its own fits when PT is the only question, for example alongside a liver result. If you take warfarin, your testing schedule and dose belong with the clinician who prescribes it.


### Von Willebrand factor antigen: the most common inherited cause


Von Willebrand factor helps platelets stick to a damaged vessel wall. The antigen test measures how much of it is in your blood. A full first workup for von Willebrand disease measures three things together: von Willebrand factor antigen, von Willebrand factor activity, and factor VIII \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33570651/) \].


Where it stops: levels vary. They run lower in people with blood group O and rise with stress, exercise, inflammation, pregnancy and estrogen, so one normal result does not exclude the condition and repeat testing is often needed \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33570651/) \]. A low[von Willebrand factor antigen result](https://mitohealth.com/products/von-willebrand-factor-antigen-vwf) is informative. A normal one is not a clearance when the bleeding history is strong.


### Liver panel: when the liver is part of the picture


The liver makes most clotting factors, which is why liver disease can lengthen clotting time \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/partial-thromboplastin-time-ptt-test/) \]. A[hepatic function panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/liver-profile) checks liver enzymes, bilirubin and proteins such as albumin. It does not measure clotting, so pair it with PT/INR when bleeding is the question \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prothrombin-time-test-and-inr-ptinr/) \]. For the wider bruising side of the same picture, see our article on[easy bruising and blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/easy-bruising-causes-blood-tests) .


### Ferritin: what repeated bleeding costs in iron


Repeated blood loss is a recognized cause of iron deficiency \[[11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30401704/) \]. Frequent nosebleeds, especially together with heavy periods, can drain iron stores slowly enough that tiredness or breathlessness never gets connected to the bleeding. Ferritin measures stored iron, and a low result points to iron deficiency \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \].


Where it stops: inflammation, such as from an infection, raises ferritin, so a normal result during an inflammatory illness can hide low stores \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]. Start with a[ferritin blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/ferritin) . The[Anemia Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/anemia-panel-b) adds a complete blood count, full iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate in one draw. See our[ferritin level guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/ferritin-level) for how to read a result and our[anemia test guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/anemia-test) for the fuller workup. If you also crave ice, our article on[craving ice](https://mitohealth.com/blog/craving-ice) explains its link to low iron.


## Medicines and supplements that make nosebleeds more likely


Blood thinners such as warfarin, antiplatelet medicines such as clopidogrel, and aspirin can cause or worsen nosebleeds \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. If you take one, a nosebleed that will not stop needs emergency care \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \], and any change to the medicine belongs with the clinician who prescribes it. Overusing decongestant nasal sprays and snorting drugs irritate the lining of the nose directly \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \].


Supplements come up often, and the evidence differs between them. High-dose vitamin E is the one with a clear caution, because it can interfere with clotting and is flagged for people taking blood thinners \[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminE-HealthProfessional/) \]. A systematic review of standardized ginkgo extract found no significant effect on bleeding risk \[[14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21923430/) \], and a large study of heart surgery patients found no increase in bleeding with fish oil \[[15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30571332/) \]. They are still worth listing for your doctor.


## Can high blood pressure cause nosebleeds?


High blood pressure and nosebleeds are linked, but a cause has not been shown. A meta-analysis of 10 studies found nosebleeds were more common in people with high blood pressure, and its authors noted that this association does not establish that high blood pressure causes them \[[16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28742425/) \]. Blood pressure is often high during a nosebleed, but the stress of the bleed itself, and anxiety in a clinic, can push the reading up, which makes a reading taken at that moment hard to interpret \[[17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23539411/) \].


The practical point: most people with high blood pressure have no symptoms, and measuring it is the only way to know \[[18](https://www.cdc.gov/high-blood-pressure/about/index.html) \]. If you have frequent nosebleeds and have not had your blood pressure checked recently, it is worth doing, for its own sake rather than to explain the nosebleeds.


## Nosebleeds in one nostril versus both


Most nosebleeds come from one nostril, usually from the front of the septum \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]. Repeated bleeding from the same side is still the common pattern. When it keeps coming back from one side despite treatment, the nosebleed guideline recommends nasal endoscopy, a look inside the nose with a thin camera, to find the bleeding site \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]. Endoscopy is also the option when a clinician is concerned about an unrecognized problem in the nose, such as a growth \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]. A blood test cannot find or rule out a growth in the nose or sinuses.


Recurrent nosebleeds from both sides, or a family history of recurrent nosebleeds, are the pattern the guideline ties to checking for HHT \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]. Bleeding from both sides can also come from a bleeding disorder, which is where the tests above apply.


## HHT: when nosebleeds run in the family


Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an inherited condition in which some blood vessels form abnormally. It affects an estimated 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000 people, and nosebleeds are very common in people who have it \[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/hereditary-hemorrhagic-telangiectasia/) \]. The small abnormal vessels near the surface, called telangiectases, appear as red markings on the skin \[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/hereditary-hemorrhagic-telangiectasia/) \], often on the lips, mouth, fingers and nose \[[20](https://curehht.org/understanding-hht/diagnosis/) \].


HHT is diagnosed from four findings: spontaneous, recurrent nosebleeds not explained by injury or dry air alone; multiple telangiectases; an abnormal vessel in an internal organ such as the lungs, brain or liver; and a first-degree relative with HHT. Three or four findings make the diagnosis definite, and genetic testing can confirm it when the picture is unclear \[[20](https://curehht.org/understanding-hht/diagnosis/) \]. Because HHT can cause chronic bleeding, international HHT guidelines include recommendations on checking for anemia and iron deficiency \[[21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32894695/) \]. Routine blood tests do not diagnose HHT, but a complete blood count and ferritin show whether the bleeding has caused anemia or low iron.


## Do frequent nosebleeds mean cancer?


Usually not. Leukemia can lower the platelet count, and frequent or severe nosebleeds, bruising and bleeding gums are among its listed signs, often alongside general symptoms such as tiredness or fever. These symptoms are more often caused by something other than leukemia \[[22](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]. A complete blood count can show abnormal blood counts that lead to further testing, but it does not diagnose or rule out cancer on its own. Our articles on[whether leukemia shows up in blood work](https://mitohealth.com/blog/does-leukemia-show-up-in-blood-work) and[early signs of leukemia in adults](https://mitohealth.com/blog/early-signs-and-symptoms-of-leukemia-in-adults) explain the details. A growth in the nose or sinuses is a less common cause of repeated nosebleeds \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \], and it is found by examining the nose, not by a blood test.


## When to see an ENT for nosebleeds


An ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist can look inside the nose and treat a bleeding vessel directly, with options such as cautery or packing \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]. A referral makes sense when:


- nosebleeds keep coming back despite earlier packing or cautery \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]
- they keep coming from the same side \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]
- they come from both sides, or relatives have recurrent nosebleeds, raising the question of HHT \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31910111/) \]
- earlier nosebleeds needed specialist treatment to stop \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003106.htm) \]


If your nosebleeds come with easy bruising, heavy periods or bleeding after dental work, a primary care doctor or hematologist can start the bleeding workup alongside the ENT visit.

## Frequently asked questions


### Can stress cause nosebleeds?


Studies have not shown that stress itself causes nosebleeds. Blood pressure is often high during a nosebleed, but researchers who reviewed the studies point out that the stress of the bleed itself can raise it, so a high reading at that moment does not show a cause. Dry air, colds, allergies, nose picking and blood thinners are the better-established triggers.


### Are nosebleeds common in pregnancy?


Yes. Nosebleeds may happen in up to 1 in 5 pregnancies, because blood volume rises and hormone changes affect the blood vessels lining the nose. The urgent-care rule is the same as for any adult: get emergency care if a nosebleed does not stop after 20 minutes of pressure. Contact your prenatal provider if nosebleeds happen often, the flow is very heavy, or you feel lightheaded or dizzy.


### Why have I suddenly started getting nosebleeds?


New nosebleeds usually follow something that changed: dry winter or indoor air, a cold or allergy season, frequent nose blowing, overuse of a decongestant nasal spray, or a new blood thinner, aspirin or clopidogrel. Nosebleeds that start without a cold or other irritation are a reason to contact your doctor, as are frequent ones.


### What can frequent nosebleeds be a sign of?


Most often, they are a sign of dry or irritated blood vessels at the front of the nose. Less often, repeated nosebleeds can be a sign of a bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease, low platelets, liver disease, the inherited blood vessel condition HHT, a medicine side effect, or rarely a growth in the nose or sinuses. Nosebleeds from both sides, long bleeds, easy bruising or heavy periods point toward a bleeding cause.


### Are blood clots from the nose after a nosebleed normal?


Yes. A clot that comes out of the nose after a nosebleed is the blood clotting as it should to seal the leak. Avoid blowing or sniffing hard for several hours afterward so the clot is not dislodged and the bleeding does not restart. The link with clots elsewhere usually runs the other way: blood thinners taken to treat or prevent clots can cause or worsen nosebleeds.
